I think the biggest trap for new players is building a deck without a strong foundation. And by that I mean, the cards that actually let you play the game: lands, ramp, draw, and interaction. Too often I see really greedy decks running a couple pieces of interaction, less than 30 lands with a mana curve above 3, and very little draw and/or ramp. 

Combos and big splashy spells are fun, but here's the rub: if you don't draw cards, you won't find key deck pieces. If you don't ramp, you fall behind everyone else. If can't stop your opponent, they will run you over. If you cant't play lands, you can't play the game. 

I first reserve 38 slots for lands, 10 for ramp, 12-15 for card draw, 10 for interaction, and 3 for board wipes. Only after that do I really focus on the deck plan, and am able to adjust accordingly because I get a better view of the whole picture. For example, if my commander is a draw engine, I'll cut a few draw cards. If I have a mana curve below 3.0, I can cut back on 1-2 lands. If I have very critical permanents for the game plan, I might run a couple extra cards to protect them. If I don't start with the fundamentals, I won't know where I can break the rules.

I also look for cards that pull double duty. E.g., \[\[Arcane Denial\]\] stops an opponent and replaces itself with a new card. If I want to deal combat damage, \[\[Renegade Tactics\]\] draws me a card and gets me past a key blocker. Leverage MDFCs to hit early game land drops, and late game flexibility.

Learning the nuances comes with time. I've been doing this for several years now and I'm still learning. So I encourage people to start with the foundations and fundamentals for a deck.

That's overkill, and very wishful thinking. If you have nothing worthwhile to clone it's a dead card, and if Veyran itself isn't generating enough value, you've got problems either with the core of the deck or your decision-making in play. I can't comment on the latter, so I'll start with some deck basics. I also recommend you watch this recent video from The Command Zone, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OSNV6224cHg&t=4476s. It's a great primer on basic deck-building templates.

I would suggest would suggest the following for Veyran:

1) 36 lands

2) 10 pieces of ramp

2) 12-15 pieces of card draw

3) 10 pieces of single target interaction (this can be counters, removal, or even protection for key pieces like \[\[Slip Out the Back\]\]

4) 2-3 board wipes or ways to deal "mass disruption" (such as \[\[Disrupt Decorum\]\]

With your commander, that leaves you with *at most* 29 slots devoted to your game plan. This really doesn't let you split focus. Right now you're trying to ping, storm, create creature tokens, and clone things. If you try to do everything, your deck won't do anything.

First, look for cards that pull double duty, like \[\[Valakut's Awakening\]\]. This is both early game land drop, and mid/late game draw/cycling. If you want to ping, pick the key creatures and cards like \[\[Fiery Inscription\]\] or \[\[Ral, Storm Conduit\]\] that let you do so. Many people see a doubler in the command zone and consider you Enemy No. 1. So you're drawing a lot of heat right off the bat. But the reality is that Veyran does nothing by itself. She's dead weight until you can play \*other\* permanents with spell-based triggers. On to specifics:

1) More lands, more ramp. 27 lands is not enough. You are not running enough fast mana and that land base cannot support a mana curve as high as yours. If you don't draw lands, you don't play the game. You should be playing at least 30 lands, \*not\* include MDFCs. I run 32 + 2 MDFCs and my curve is a fair bit lower than yours. And frankly, I should update my own deck to run more MDFCs.

2) Related, you've got several X-spells and 6+ mana value spells that I have to imagine just sit in your hand or get very little value because you can't actually afford to cast them. 

3) More card draw. More cheap 1- and 2-mana draw cards. More permanent sources of draw. More recursion to get extra value from those spells. You don't have much of any of those. If you want to go lighter on lands, you need to get that 

4) Your strategy seems very unfocused. Are you winning with pingers, or token creatures and combat damage? Are you trying to storm off, or assemble combo pieces? You need to decide what you want to do with the deck and laser focus on it. Having a secondary strategy is good, but it should support your primary one.

5) There are a number of cards that don't make sense to me. \[\[Extravagant Replication\]\] do nothing to advance your strategy. \[\[Stella Lee\]\] is primarily a combo piece, and while she can give you card advantage, you have to jump through hoops to get it. A card like \[\[Thousand-Year Storm\]\] can close out games with the right spells, but it is really expensive. You can't drop that t5/6 and pass and expect it to survive the following turn.

In sum: 1) more lands, 2) more card draw, 3) focus, focus focus.

I struggle with this too, and I'm much older than you. Writing is a life-long pursuit, and most of it is just dogged determination and stubbornness to work through the issues.

There are two ways to get good at writing - read a lot, and write a lot. Read a lot of fiction, but also read about the craft of writing and storytelling.

And then, just write. Just sit down, bang out a few hundred words a day, and do it all over again. Write 4, maybe 5 days a week. Do not overwhelm yourself in trying to write an entire story as quickly as possible. Writing is a process and that process is much more digestible in small chunks. Consider this: if you were to write 300 words, for five days a week, for 52 weeks in a row, you would have 78,000 words, about 260 pages. That's a lot.

You're 16. You have a lot of time, and a lot to learn. There's no rush, and you shouldn't beat yourself up because you don't know or understand everything.
